gao-gaoreports-gao-05-218g:
Framework for Assessing the Acquisition Function at Federal Agencies, GAO-05-218G of September 1, 2005, is a tool, not a probe. Agencies lean more and more on firms to do their work. Hundreds of billions of tax dollars buy goods and services each year. Weak buying wastes that cash. Buying at some agencies sits on GAO's high-risk list.

The framework rests on four linked stones. They are fit structure and strong lead, sound rules and steps, skilled staff, and good grip on facts. Top chiefs can grade their own shops with it. Watch groups can aim their probes with it. Each stone can stand alone for a tight check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-568g: Guidance for auditors on the training duties in the federal audit rulebook is the whole of GAO-05-568G, issued on April 1, 2005. The short document, put out by the Comptroller General, helps auditors and audit organizations put the continuing professional education requirements of the 2003 revision of Government Auditing Standards into practice. Its indexed topics run to auditing standards, continuing education, and the Yellow Book. The hosted text is the guidance statement itself, in brief form.
uslaw-usc-t2-s288g:
Section 288g of Title 2 assigns advisory and cooperative duties to the Senate Legal Counsel. The Counsel shall advise, consult, and cooperate with a list of offices and persons. The first named is the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia, on criminal proceedings for contempt of Congress certified by the Senate.

The list continues with the Senate committee charged with spotting court actions of vital interest to the Senate. It also names the Comptroller General, the Government Accountability Office, the Office of Legislative Counsel, and the Congressional Research Service. A guard clause protects those offices, so the Counsel's duties do not cut into theirs. Help for Members in obtaining private legal counsel is also in view. The section sits in Chapter 9D of Title 2, on the Office of Senate Legal Counsel. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s658g:
Section 658g of Title 2 of the United States Code says when a mandates part applies. The part sits in the rules on Congress and its budget work. It can reach a bill, a joint measure, an amendment, or a motion. A conference report on such a measure is in the same reach.

The part applies only when a set effect would follow from passage. One trigger is a net cut in funds for federal aid. That aid helps states, towns, or tribes meet a federal mandate's terms. Aid to the private sector for the same end is in the rule. The cut must not be matched by a like cut in the duties set. A net rise in the cost of federal mandates is the second trigger named.
